questions.topic: Why a limit keyed on one account is not a limit on one person
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an account limit does not bound a person
questions.stem: Explain to the survey lead why a per-account upload quota does not limit what one researcher can send.

answer.exemplar: The quota is attached to the account, and the account is attached to the key or token that the software uses. A researcher who signs in on several devices, or who shares a station token with colleagues, presents the same quota several times over, and a team that pools one account spreads the work of many people behind a single allowance. The limit therefore bounds a credential rather than a person, and the only way to make it a limit on people is to bind it to something they cannot duplicate.

questions.explanation: The quota counts accounts, and a person can hold several accounts or share one. A limit on accounts is therefore not a limit on people.
questions.hint: Ask what the quota is actually keyed on.

questions.topic: What a sliding window log buys and what it costs in memory
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a sliding window log provides and what it costs
questions.stem: Explain to the team what a sliding window log gives the quota service and what it costs in memory.

answer.exemplar: Keeping a log of recent timestamps lets the service apply the limit to any window of the last minute rather than to a fixed block, so a client cannot send its whole allowance at the end of one block and again at the start of the next. The cost is that one timestamp must be held per request inside the window, so a busy service keeps a great many small entries in memory, and the work of discarding expired entries must happen on every check rather than once at the boundary.

questions.explanation: The log makes the limit apply to any rolling window, so boundary bursts no longer work. The price is one stored timestamp per request inside the window.
questions.hint: Ask how many timestamps the service must hold.

questions.stem: Explain to a reviewer what a bounded queue changes about the way a failure travels through a pipeline.

answer.exemplar: An unbounded queue has no limit on how much work it will hold, so when the stage behind it slows down the backlog grows without limit and the failure travels upstream until the components at the front exhaust their own memory or disk. The failure no longer travels, but it is also no longer silent: something has to be thrown away, and the bound decides how much and which.

answer.exemplar: A retry loop with no attempt limit and no delay keeps asking a service that is already unwell, and each attempt consumes capacity that the service needed in order to recover. questions.stem: Explain to the field team why a counter that resets on a fixed boundary can be overrun.

answer.exemplar: A fixed window counter starts a fresh allowance at every boundary, and it checks each request against the allowance for the block it falls in. A client that spends its whole allowance just before a boundary gets a fresh allowance immediately afterwards, so in a few seconds around the boundary it can send twice the intended rate. The limit is still respected inside each block, which is why the behaviour is easy to miss in testing; it only appears when traffic is timed to the boundary.

questions.explanation: The counter checks each request against the block it lands in, so a client can spend the allowance twice around a boundary. The limit holds inside each block and fails between them.
questions.hint: Ask what a client can do right before the counter resets.

answer.exemplar: Exponential backoff sets the wait for attempt n as a multiple of the base delay that grows with each failure, which stops a client from hammering a service that is unwell. questions.learningObjective: Identify the boundary overrun a reset permits
questions.stem: A quota service intends to limit clients to 100 uploads per minute, but its counter resets when the minute changes, and a station sends 95 uploads in the last seconds of a minute.

options.text: The bug lets that station send 95 more immediately, so it uses 190 in two minutes
The bug is harmless, because 95 uploads is below the limit of 100 in any window
options.misconception: checks only the first burst against the limit

options.text: The bug only affects clients that upload near the hour, because the counter resets hourly
options.misconception: invents an hourly reset on a per-minute counter

options.text: The bug is fixed by lowering the limit to 50 uploads per minute for every client
options.misconception: cures a boundary problem by halving the allowance

questions.explanation: The reset hands out a fresh allowance immediately, so the same station can use its allowance twice within seconds. The limit holds inside each block and fails between them.
questions.hint: Ask what the station can do right after the reset.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What load shedding protects that queueing does not
questions.learningObjective: Explain what load shedding protects over queueing
questions.stem: A reviewer asks what load shedding protects that leaving the work in the queue does not.

options.text: Load shedding protects the sender, because fewer readings are accepted so the sender can transmit faster
options.misconception: claims shedding benefits the producer

options.text: Load shedding protects the processing capacity, because excess work is refused rather than accumulated
Load shedding protects the disk, because queued readings are never written to the log
options.misconception: claims the queue is never persisted

options.text: Load shedding protects the reading accuracy, because dropped readings are later re-sent
options.misconception: invents automatic re-sending of shed work

questions.explanation: Shedding refuses work that would only wait, so processors and memory stay free for work that can be completed. Queueing keeps everything and consumes both.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to work that would only wait anyway.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why an unbounded retry loop turns a small fault into an outage
questions.learningObjective: Count how many retries fit inside a fault window
questions.stem: A station's retry policy allows 5 attempts with a delay that doubles from 4 seconds. The station's uplink fails for 2 minutes, and the reviewer asks how many attempts fit in that window.

options.text: Six attempts, because the attempt that starts at 124 seconds still counts as inside the window
options.misconception: counts an attempt beyond the window

options.text: Five attempts, because the waits of 4, 8, 16 and 32 seconds place attempts at 0, 4, 12, 28 and 60 seconds
Three attempts, because only the first three waits of 4, 8 and 16 seconds fit inside two minutes
options.misconception: stops counting once the waits get large

options.text: Seven attempts, because the policy counts the attempt after the window as part of it
options.misconception: counts attempts beyond the window

questions.explanation: The waits place attempts at 0, 4, 12, 28 and 60 seconds, and the next would be at 124 seconds, so five attempts fall inside the two minutes.
questions.hint: Add the doubling waits to find each attempt's time.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a limit keyed on one account is not a limit on one person
questions.learningObjective: Describe what would make a quota follow a person
questions.stem: Ask the team to explain what it would take for an upload quota to be a limit on a person rather than on an account.

answer.exemplar: A quota counted against an account bounds the credentials, and credentials are cheap: one person can hold several accounts or share a team one, so the effective allowance multiplies without any change in the number of people uploading. To make the limit follow a person the quota has to be attached to something that cannot be duplicated or shared, such as a named licence, a personal device registration, or a per-person allocation agreed with the survey lead. The cost of that is administrative, and the benefit is that the number in the policy means what everyone assumes it means.

questions.explanation: An account is a credential, and a person can hold several or share one. Bounding people requires a key that cannot be duplicated, and that costs administration.
questions.hint: Ask what cannot be duplicated or shared.
